chat_history.content: Can you explain the Dilation curve?

The dilation curve describes how segmented voxel counts — and measured co-localization between channels — change as a radial dilation radius is applied around each segmented object. At the current stats_radius_um of 8.39 µm, each segmented cell mask is expanded outward by that distance before overlap is computed, meaning the statistics capture not just direct cell-body co-expression but also close spatial proximity within roughly one cell diameter. For MX1 (yellow, 2.14 billion segmented voxels) and MHC-I (magenta, 2.19 billion segmented voxels) across this viewport, the dilation radius determines whether two nearby but non-overlapping cells are counted as co-localizing: a smaller radius yields only true intracellular co-expression, while a larger radius increasingly captures cell–cell neighborhood relationships. MX1 and MHC-I do not appear in the combinations list at this radius, which suggests that even with 8.39 µm dilation their signals are not among the strongest overlapping pairs in this region — the dominant overlaps are structural/ubiquitous markers (COX-IV, B-tubulin, B-actin, Hoechst/lamin-ABC), indicating that MX1 and MHC-I occupy spatially distinct subpopulations rather than a tightly co-expressing phenotype. To map the full dilation curve, one would compare overlap_coeff and iou for MX1/MHC-I across multiple radius values: rising overlap_coeff with increasing radius would indicate a paracrine or juxtacrine interferon-signaling relationship rather than cell-intrinsic co-regulation.
